The greatest paradox of the silver market is that the price of the physical metal is not determined by how many bars mines produce or how much factories consume.
The price (the so-called "spot" price) is almost entirely dictated by trading on futures exchanges—primarily the COMEX in New York—and the over-the-counter (OTC) market in London.
• Financial institutions (major bullion banks, investment funds) can create millions of ounces of so-called "paper silver" with just a few mouse clicks.
• If these banks flood the market with a billion ounces in short contracts ("shorting"), the exchange price drops.
• A mine in Peru or Poland (such as KGHM) has no choice: it must sell its actual, mined silver at the price set by a computer in New York or London—even if there is a shortage of the physical metal in the market.

2. Why are physical producers’ hands tied?

Miners and processors of the physical commodity operate under immense capital pressure, forcing them to play by the rules imposed by the banking system:
• Mines are compelled to sell at low prices: Most mines require a steady cash flow to cover ongoing operations (wages, energy, machinery). They cannot afford to stockpile silver and wait for "better times." Furthermore, the banks that finance the construction of these mines often mandate hedging agreements—contracts that require the sale of future output at predetermined, low exchange-based prices. • Electronics/renewable energy manufacturers cannot compete with banks: a technology corporation is subject to rigorous audits and tax regulations (established in the U.S.?). Bullion banks, by contrast, operate within clearing systems and have direct access to nearly cost-free liquidity (e.g., loans from central banks), which allows them to maintain massive positions in the futures market without the risk of operational bankruptcy.

3. The Role of Governments and Regulators (U.S. Perspective)

For the U.S. government and the Federal Reserve (Fed), the stability of the system of paper-based commodity contracts is of strategic importance:
• Protecting the dollar: If the prices of gold and silver were to begin rising rapidly and uncontrollably, it would expose the decline in the dollar’s ​​purchasing power (inflation). Controlling commodity prices through futures markets helps maintain confidence in fiat currency.
• Regulatory asymmetry: There have been instances in history (such as the famous "Silver Thursday" involving the Hunt brothers in 1980) where private investors attempted to buy up physical silver and challenge the system. In such cases, the COMEX exchange—with the approval of regulators—was able to change the rules of the game overnight, for example by drastically increasing margin requirements or prohibiting the opening of new long (buy) positions, while allowing only sales. This effectively broke the back of the upward price trend.

🔍 Where is this leading? The current system has created a massive asymmetry: financiers profit from trading a virtual commodity, while the real economy—mines and factories producing renewable energy infrastructure—bears the entire risk of physical labor.
However, this dynamic holds only as long as the physical commodity does not run out entirely. Once industrial demand finally exceeds the supply available in vaults—a scenario signaled by a six-year-long deficit—the banks' paper-based manipulations will lose their efficacy, and the true value of a physical bullion bar will diverge sharply from the price displayed on stock exchange screens.
